title: What Actually Hit Tunguska in 1908?
parts: In nineteen oh eight, something exploded over Siberia with the force of a nuclear bomb.
It flattened over two thousand square kilometers of forest.
And to this day, there is no crater.
Scientists have studied the site for over a century, and they still cannot agree on one basic question.
What actually hit the Earth that morning.
We will mark every claim: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you will see the clue that rules out a simple rock.
You will hear how the official energy estimate for the blast was quietly cut in half, twice.
And you will find out why the only real victims of this event are almost never mentioned.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
June thirtieth, nineteen oh eight. Around seven fourteen in the morning, local time.
The location: the basin of the Podkamennaya Tunguska River, in central Siberia.
Today that region sits inside Russia's Krasnoyarsk Krai.
Documented.
The blast flattened an area of more than two thousand square kilometers of forest.
The trees fell outward, in a radial pattern people compare to a pair of wings.
You will often hear a count near eighty million trees. Sources call that figure a repeated overestimate, without giving a replacement number.
The true count stays uncertain. The scale does not.
Here is the detail that still surprises people.
There is no crater.
At the very center, an area about eight kilometers across, trees were left standing. Stripped of their branches, but standing.
A Russian scientist named Kulik led expeditions there in nineteen twenty one and nineteen twenty seven, searching for the crater. He never found one.

Later teams found dozens of odd pools that looked like craters. One, nicknamed after a researcher called Suslov, had a tree stump sitting at its bottom. That ruled out a meteorite for that pool, at least.
This event is often described as striking an empty wilderness.
It did not.

At least three people from the local Evenki community died: two from injuries or shock, one likely in a forest fire the blast caused. Around thirty more people were exposed to the shockwave, several losing consciousness. Reindeer and dogs were killed too. Windows broke as far as two hundred kilometers away.
These were real people, in a real place. Documented.
For decades, textbooks gave one number for the blast: somewhere between ten and twenty megatons.
In two thousand seven, a team at Sandia National Laboratories ran a new three-dimensional supercomputer simulation.
Their revised estimate: closer to three to five megatons. Less than half the old textbook number.
The reason: older models ignored how the asteroid's motion interacted with the shockwave, and how hills amplified the damage on the ground. Documented.
So if the energy number kept shrinking, what actually exploded?
Here is where the real mystery sits.

In twenty twenty, a Russian research team proposed something unusual: an iron asteroid, fifty to two hundred meters across, that skimmed through the atmosphere without ever touching the ground, and kept going.
That would explain the missing crater. The authors call it a model that supports their idea, not a confirmed fact.
A separate two thousand thirteen analysis of tiny fragments found at the site leaned toward an iron meteorite too.
But a whole different line of research points to a comet instead, a case made since nineteen thirty four and argued over ever since. Nobody has closed this debate. Disputed.
One explanation you will see online: that Nikola Tesla's Wardenclyffe Tower caused the blast.
According to that story, Tesla's death ray misfired and struck Siberia by accident.
The problem: Wardenclyffe could never have produced anywhere near the power needed for an explosion that size, according to multiple writers who have examined the claim.
Myth. Tesla did write to newspapers about a long range weapon, but nothing connects it to this event.
Let's count what we actually know.
The date, the place, the missing crater: documented.
The lower energy estimate from two thousand seven: documented.
What actually exploded, rock or ice or iron: still disputed. The Tesla explanation: a myth.
So, more than a hundred years later, what hit Tunguska?
Nobody knows for certain. Not historians, not physicists, not the scientists still publishing new models today.
Sometimes the mystery really does stay open. And maybe that is the more honest story.
